verdict.rationale: Both PRs find the real cause: the CRM file uses `customer_id`, so CRM customers were indexed under `undefined`. Both fix it at load time without touching the data files. A also switches the export to the existing `requireCustomer`. A truly unknown customer then gives the README's `UnknownReferenceError`, with exit status 1 and nothing on stdout, instead of a TypeError. That reuses existing code to meet the stated convention for exactly the failure the user hit. B handles the loader more cleanly and has robust data tests, but it knowingly leaves the export able to crash with a raw stack trace on a real data error.
a_issues: `tests/sources.test.js` reads `"data"` relative to the working directory, so it only passes when tests run from the repository root.
The doc comment on `loadCustomerRecords` grew into one long line, and the CRM mapping is written inline instead of in a named helper.
b_issues: The export still uses `customers.get`, so an invoice whose customer is truly unknown still crashes with an uncaught TypeError. This goes against the README rule that such references raise `UnknownReferenceError` and exit 1. The report acknowledges this but defers it.
No test covers what the export does when a customer is missing.

verdict.rationale: Both changes fix the actual cause the same way: CRM records are mapped from `customer_id` to `customerId` at load time, which brings back all 8 invoices including INV-1041. B also replaces the bare `customers.get` in `invoiceRow` with the existing `requireCustomer` helper. A genuinely missing customer then raises `UnknownReferenceError`, which the CLI reports cleanly with exit status 1 and no output, exactly as the README requires, instead of the TypeError crash the user hit. A sees this gap and openly leaves it, so the export path still crashes with a stack trace on bad data, against the documented convention. B's addition is one line, reuses existing code and has its own test.
